query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: At elevated temperatures, the inherent microstructural heterogeneity in a multi‐phase eutectic HEA (with alternating soft and hard phases) promotes differential oxidation kinetics and micro‐galvanic coupling at phase boundaries. During cyclic sliding in a corrosive (chloride-containing) environment, the initially protective oxide films formed on the individual phases are repeatedly disrupted by wear stresses. This spallation exposes the adjacent, compositionally distinct phases to aggressive localized corrosion (e.g., pitting) at the interfaces. The accelerated corrosion weakens the material locally, which in turn enhances abrasive and adhesive wear, establishing a positive feedback loop that drives the overall rapid coupled degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high-entropy alloy exhibiting a lamellar microstructure with alternating phases (e.g., FCC and BCC/σ phases) that differ in composition and oxidation behavior.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to simultaneous reciprocating or sliding wear under corrosive conditions (e.g., in a chloride-containing environment) at elevated temperatures (e.g., 700–900 °C).
generation.conditions: Atmospheric or molten salt conditions that promote oxidation (oxygen present) and chloride-induced corrosion, combined with high temperature (≥700 °C) and cyclic mechanical loading that induces frictional heating and mechanical stresses.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase boundaries and lamellar interfaces between dissimilar phases in the eutectic microstructure that provide sites for galvanic coupling and differential oxide formation.
generation.mechanism: Under high-temperature cyclic loading in a corrosive environment, protective oxide films forming on individual phases become mechanically unstable and spall off. The repeated exposure of galvanically coupled phase interfaces (due to compositional contrast) accelerates localized corrosion (e.g., pitting at phase boundaries). This corrosion degrades the phase integrity, making the material more susceptible to further wear. The synergy between wear-induced oxide disruption and galvanic corrosion leads to overall accelerated degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline with a more homogeneous or stabilized microstructure (e.g., after treatments that reduce phase boundary area), the original multi-phase eutectic HEA is expected to show an increased total degradation rate, with both higher wear volume loss and an increased density of corrosion pits. Individually, the wear response will shift toward more abrasive and adhesive spallation damage, while the corrosion response will show more prominent pitting localized at phase interfaces.
generation.baseline: A matched HEA sample with either a homogenized microstructure (minimized compositional heterogeneity at phase boundaries) or one processed to yield more stable oxide films, tested under identical elevated-temperature, corrosive wear conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under conditions where high temperatures (≥700 °C) elevate oxidation rates and mechanical wear stresses are sufficient to disrupt protective films in a chloride-laden environment that fosters galavanic corrosion. The effect may be less pronounced at lower temperatures or in less aggressive corrosive media.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal integrates evidence of wear-induced oxide spallation and mechanically activated tribo-oxidation (PMC12156342::web::036, PMC10241162::web::000, PMC10241162::web::015) with findings on phase-specific localized corrosion and galvanic effects in eutectic HEAs (PMC12735082::web::000, PMC9319277::web::022). While the qualitative interplay is supported, the quantitative contribution of each mechanism (oxide instability versus galvanic coupling) and their precise rate dependencies remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of eutectic HEA samples: one group with standard as-cast lamellar microstructure and another group treated (e.g., via post-heat treatment or thermomechanical processing) to minimize phase boundary density and promote a more homogeneous oxide film formation. Expose both groups to identical high-temperature (e.g., 900 °C) simultaneous wear and corrosive conditions (using a controlled chloride environment with similar mechanical loading).
measurements: Quantitative wear volume loss using laser scanning microscopy
Corrosion pit density and depth via SEM and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy
Characterization of oxide film integrity and spallation using XRD and SEM
Measurement of friction coefficients during tribological testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the microstructurally homogenized samples (with reduced phase boundaries) do not exhibit significantly lower combined degradation (i.e., similar wear volume and corrosion pit density as the standard eutectic samples), then the hypothesis—that phase-boundary-mediated galvanic coupling coupled with wear-induced oxide spallation drives the accelerated degradation—is refuted.
